analysis.one_liner: Lets state and local police enforce federal immigration law and dramatically expands detention, deportation, and criminal penalties for immigrants.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved this enforcement-only immigration bill on a 20-15 party-line vote in June 2013, but it was not reported until the final weeks of 2014 and never received a vote in the full House or Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Act would overhaul immigration enforcement. It would let every state and local police department arrest people for immigration violations, let states write their own criminal immigration laws, make being in the country without papers a crime, expand the list of offenses (including a second drunk-driving conviction) that trigger automatic detention and permanent banishment, build new detention facilities, and cut federal grant money from any city or state that limits cooperation with immigration agents. It would also strip courts of much of their ability to review visa denials and immigration decisions, and let federal border agents bypass land-management rules within 100 miles of the border. The House Judiciary Committee approved it on a party-line vote in 2013, but it was never brought to a vote in the full House or Senate before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill's main beneficiaries would be the agencies and contractors of the immigration enforcement system: private and public operators of detention facilities (the bill requires construction of new detention beds and allows private detention contracts), ICE (hundreds of new deportation officers, prosecutors, and detention officers), and state and local police departments, which would receive federal grants, reimbursement of incarceration costs, and immunity from lawsuits while enforcing immigration law. State governments that adopt aggressive local immigration enforcement would gain federal money and legal cover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: ICE, detention contractors, and state police agencies

how_it_helps.text: It lets state and local police enforce federal immigration law and lets states write their own criminal immigration penalties, effectively deputizing every local officer as an immigration agent [S2, S3].

It greatly expands the list of crimes—going back retroactively for years—that make an immigrant deportable or permanently inadmissible, and expands mandatory and potentially indefinite detention [S3].

It makes unlawfully being in the United States itself a federal crime, criminalizes transporting or even 'encouraging' an undocumented immigrant, and directs construction of new detention facilities plus hundreds of additional ICE officers [S2, S3].
It gives federal agents authority to ignore land-management rules on federal lands within 100 miles of the border and cuts off federal law-enforcement grants to 'sanctuary' jurisdictions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Immigrants—including many who are longtime residents with U.S.-citizen children—would bear the cost through criminal prosecution for unlawful presence, mandatory and potentially indefinite detention, expanded retroactive deportation grounds, and loss of access to asylum and other relief. Taxpayers would fund new detention facilities, expanded ICE staffing, and grants to state and local police. Ordinary communities would also bear the cost of local police being drawn into federal immigration enforcement, which discourages immigrants from reporting crimes or cooperating as witnesses.

drawbacks.text: It criminalizes unlawful presence itself—currently a civil violation—so simply being in the country without papers would become a crime, and it makes a second drunk-driving conviction an 'aggravated felony,' a label that carries mandatory detention and a permanent bar on ever legalizing status [S3].

Many provisions apply retroactively: crimes and immigration violations from decades past, including conduct before 1996, would trigger deportation, and indefinite detention is authorized for people who cannot be removed while courts are stripped of much of their power to review visa denials, naturalization decisions, and detention [S3, S4].

It strips courts of jurisdiction to review many immigration decisions—including visa revocation and delayed background checks—which removes a basic check on executive error even for people with strong claims [S3, S4].

It directs federal agents to override environmental and land-management protections within 100 miles of the borders, waiving normal limits on road construction and patrols on national parks and forests [S3].

Even supporters would acknowledge the fiscal cost: new detention facilities, thousands of additional ICE officers, federal reimbursement of state incarceration costs, and grants to local police all draw on appropriations with no offsets identified in the bill [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated targets—criminal aliens, gang members, visa fraud—address real public safety concerns, and some provisions (a biometric entry-exit system, student-visa fraud controls) are defensible on their own terms. But the costs are broad and severe: it criminalizes ordinary unlawful presence, makes relatively minor and old offenses grounds for permanent banishment with no chance to argue individual circumstances, puts everyday local policing in the business of immigration enforcement (which tends to make immigrant communities afraid to report crimes or cooperate with police), and locks in expensive detention infrastructure. It was an enforcement-only bill with no legalization pathway attached, so its benefits are narrow while its burdens fall on millions of families and on taxpayers funding the expansion.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it on a 20-15 vote in 2013, but it was not formally reported and placed on the House calendar until the last month of the Congress, and the full House and Senate never voted on it before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in June 2013 and ordered reported by the Judiciary Committee on a 20-15 vote the same month, but the committee did not actually file its report until December 16, 2014—over a year later [S6].

On the day it was reported, it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting a floor vote in the House; it received no further action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S6].
The bill never received a vote in the full House and was never taken up by the Senate, so it died without a floor vote in either chamber [S1, S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Immigrant families and communities are spared the bill's expanded criminal penalties and detention; the enforcement-first agenda it represented made no headway into law, while members of Congress who campaigned on it could still cite its committee approval.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Immigrant communities; the bill died without a vote

for.name: Trey Gowdy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 6, 2013 and shepherded it through the Judiciary Committee

for.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
for.what_they_did: Held a markup and ordered the bill reported amended on a 20-15 vote on June 18, 2013; formally reported it on December 16, 2014

for.name: 39 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 39 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican: the bill had 39 Republican cosponsors and passed the Judiciary Committee 20-15, with committee Democrats voting no; no Democrat sponsored it.

industries.industry: Private prison and immigrant detention contractors
industries.note: The bill requires construction or acquisition of new detention facilities and expands mandatory and potentially indefinite detention, guaranteeing more detainees and more contracts. Immigration attorneys note the bill text even contemplates private contracts to run transfers.

Police departments gain federal grants for equipment, reimbursement of incarceration and transportation costs, and legal immunity for immigration enforcement they perform. Communities where immigrants fear reporting crimes bear the cost.

industries.industry: Border enforcement and surveillance technology firms
industries.note: The bill mandates a biometric entry-exit system at every port of entry within two years, funds detention and patrol infrastructure, and expands CBP access to federal lands—all of which funnel money to contractors in these sectors.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities enrolling foreign students
industries.note: The bill tightens accreditation, background-check, and fraud-suspension rules for schools hosting foreign students, raising compliance costs while arguably protecting the integrity of the student-visa program.
